title: Ezekiel 8:1–6
context: Ezekiel 8:1–6 opens a long vision that runs through chapter 11, told by the prophet in the first person. In the sixth year, sixth month, fifth day, as Ezekiel sat in his house with the elders of Judah before him, the Lord GOD’s hand fell on him (8:1). The year is generally reckoned, as in 1:2, from King Jehoiachin’s exile, though conversions to a modern calendar are discussed rather than settled. Ezekiel sees a figure of fire and gleaming brightness (8:2; compare 1:27), who takes him by a lock of his hair; the Spirit lifts him between earth and sky and brings him “in the visions of God” to Jerusalem (8:3). This is a visionary journey; the text does not suggest that Ezekiel left Babylon in body, and he is returned to the exiles at the vision’s end (11:24). At the north gate of the inner court stands “the seat of the image of jealousy, which provokes to jealousy” (8:3, 5). What the image was is not stated; some readers connect it with the image Manasseh set in the temple (2 Kings 21:7; 2 Chronicles 33:7, 15), but that is a suggestion, and the name may describe its effect, provoking the LORD who calls himself “a jealous God” (Exodus 20:5). The glory of the God of Israel is there, as Ezekiel saw it in the plain (8:4; compare 3:23). The LORD addresses Ezekiel as son of man, a form of address used throughout the book that stresses the prophet’s human frailty before God; later uses of the phrase, as in Daniel 7:13 and the Gospels, are a separate question, left for those passages. The LORD asks whether Ezekiel sees the great abominations that would drive him far from his sanctuary, and promises to show him greater ones (8:6). Both traditions read the scene soberly as shared ground, holding that idolatry at the heart of worship provokes the LORD and prepares for the departure of his glory.

verses.text: In the sixth year, in the sixth month, in the fifth day of the month, as I sat in my house, and the elders of Judah sat before me, the Lord GOD’s hand fell on me there.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel dates the vision to the sixth year, sixth month, fifth day, as he sat in his house with the elders of Judah before him. Arminian readers note that the elders come to the prophet seeking a word, and they see God meeting his people in exile even while their homeland is under judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the date is generally reckoned from Jehoiachin’s exile, as in 1:2, though its modern equivalent is discussed. They observe that the Lord GOD’s hand falling on Ezekiel marks the vision as God’s initiative, and they read the setting among the elders as shared ground.

verses.text: Then I saw, and behold, a likeness as the appearance of fire—from the appearance of his waist and downward, fire, and from his waist and upward, as the appearance of brightness, as it were glowing metal.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel sees a likeness like fire from the waist down and brightness like glowing metal from the waist up. Arminian readers note the close resemblance to the figure of 1:27, named without harmonizing, and they see the same glorious presence now appearing to show the prophet what is happening in Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo of chapter 1 and the restraint of the description, which speaks of likeness and appearance rather than describing God directly. They read the verse as shared ground on the holiness of the One who reveals the people’s sin to the prophet.

verses.text: He stretched out the form of a hand, and took me by a lock of my head; and the Spirit lifted me up between earth and the sky, and brought me in the visions of God to Jerusalem, to the door of the gate of the inner court that looks toward the north, where there was the seat of the image of jealousy, which provokes to jealousy.
verses.arminianNotes: The figure takes Ezekiel by a lock of his hair, and the Spirit brings him “in the visions of God” to Jerusalem, to the seat of the image of jealousy. Arminian readers note that this is a visionary journey and that the image’s identity is uncertain, though some connect it with Manasseh’s image (2 Kings 21:7).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the journey as visionary and hold the identification of the image loosely. They observe that the name image of jealousy may describe its effect, provoking the LORD who calls himself “a jealous God” (Exodus 20:5), and they read the verse soberly as shared ground.

verses.text: Behold, the glory of the God of Israel was there, according to the appearance that I saw in the plain.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel says the glory of the God of Israel was there, as he had seen it in the plain. Arminian readers note the link with 3:23, named without harmonizing, and they see the sharp contrast between the LORD’s glory and the idol standing nearby in the same courts of his house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same contrast and observe that the glory is still present in the temple at this point in the vision. They read the verse as preparing for the departure of the glory in the chapters that follow, a movement both traditions read as shared ground.

verses.text: Then he said to me, “Son of man, lift up your eyes now the way toward the north.” So I lifted up my eyes the way toward the north, and saw, northward of the gate of the altar this image of jealousy in the entry.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Son of man, lift up your eyes now the way toward the north”, and Ezekiel sees the image of jealousy at the entry by the gate of the altar. Arminian readers note that son of man is a form of address stressing the prophet’s humanity, and they read the scene soberly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same form of address and decline to build an argument from it here. They observe that the image stands near the altar, at the heart of Israel’s worship, and they read the placement as showing how deeply idolatry had entered the life of the temple.

verses.text: He said to me, “Son of man, do you see what they do? Even the great abominations that the house of Israel commit here, that I should go far off from my sanctuary? But you will again see yet other great abominations.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks, “Son of man, do you see what they do?” and speaks of great abominations “that I should go far off from my sanctuary”. Arminian readers note the grief implied in God being driven from his own house, and they see the people’s choices as the cause of his departure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same link between abomination and the glory’s departure, and they read it as God’s righteous withdrawal from a defiled sanctuary. Both traditions see the promise of yet other great abominations as leading the prophet deeper into the extent of Judah’s sin.
